# Pointwise is not uniform

## Beat 1 — Where the cutoff may depend on x

Content needed: State pointwise convergence as ∀x∈D ∀ε>0 ∃N ∀n≥N: |f_n(x)−f(x)|<ε, and uniform convergence as ∀ε>0 ∃N ∀x∈D ∀n≥N: |f_n(x)−f(x)|<ε. N is a positive integer. Emphasize allowed dependence N(x,ε) versus N(ε); keep the same error inequality.

Narration: Pointwise convergence means this: for every point x and every positive tolerance epsilon, there is an integer cutoff N such that, for all n at least N, the distance between f sub n of x and f of x is less than epsilon.

Narration: Uniform convergence means that for every positive tolerance epsilon, there is one cutoff N that works for every x in the domain and every n at least N.

Narration: The error test is identical. What changes is when we must choose the cutoff. Pointwise, we may first inspect x and then choose N. Uniformly, we must choose N before knowing which x will be tested. A collection of successful individual choices need not contain one choice that works everywhere. Let us see exactly where that can fail.

## Beat 2 — Keep the endpoint

Content needed: Introduce f_n(x)=x^n for positive integers n on [0,1]. Show selected curves n=1,2,8,32. Derive the pointwise limit f(x)=0 for 0≤x<1 and f(1)=1. In the limit graph, use an open point at (1,0) and filled point at (1,1). Inspect x=1/2 and x=1 separately. Do not substitute distance to zero for error at x=1.

Narration: Take f sub n of x equal to x to the n, on the closed interval from zero to one. At one half, repeated powers approach zero. The same happens at every fixed x strictly below one: powers of a nonnegative number smaller than one tend to zero. At zero, they are already zero.

Narration: But at one, every power is one. So our pointwise limit is zero everywhere below one, and one at the endpoint. That endpoint belongs to the domain; we cannot quietly remove it.

Narration: Now measure error against this actual limit. Below one, the error is x to the n. At one, the error is zero, because both functions equal one. The difficulty must therefore come from points near the endpoint, rather than the endpoint itself.

## Beat 3 — A moving witness

Content needed: For every positive integer n define x_n=(1/2)^(1/n), strictly below one, so x_n^n=1/2. Use ε=1/4. Withhold the prediction's answer until Reveal. Then demonstrate that any proposed N fails already at n=N and x=x_N. Show uniform error E_n=sup_{x∈[0,1]}|x^n−f(x)|=1; this supremum is not attained. Distinguish the changing witness x_n from a fixed x.

Narration: For any positive n, choose x to be the nth root of one half. This point lies strictly below one, and raising it to the nth power gives one half. Its limit value is zero, so its error is one half.

Invitation (spoken): Predict whether any cutoff can make every error smaller than one quarter. Take a few seconds to use this chosen point.

Pause: 5s

Reveal (spoken): No cutoff can work. Whatever cutoff N you propose, take n equal to N and choose that corresponding root. The error is still one half, exceeding one quarter.

Narration: The chosen point changes with n, approaching one. This does not contradict pointwise convergence, which keeps x fixed while n grows. In fact, for every n, errors below one approach one as x approaches one. Their supremum is one, although no point attains it. That uniform error never tends to zero.

## Beat 4 — One bound for the whole interval

Content needed: Restrict the same sequence to [0,a] with fixed 0<a<1. Its pointwise limit is now zero everywhere, and E_n=sup_{x∈[0,a]}x^n=a^n→0. Derive 0≤x^n≤a^n and choose N with a^N<ε; for n≥N, a^n≤a^N<ε. Use a=0.9 and ε=1/4 as an optional visible concrete instance: N=14 works since 0.9^14≈0.229. The bound and cutoff may depend on fixed a and ε, but not x. Conclude the quantifier comparison on this construction.

Narration: Now restrict the domain to the interval from zero to a, where a is fixed and strictly less than one. The pointwise limit is zero throughout this interval.

Narration: Every x is at most a, so every error is at most a to the n. This time the supremum is exactly a to the n, attained at a. And that bound tends to zero.

Narration: Given any positive epsilon, choose N so that a to the N is smaller than epsilon. For every n at least N, and every x in our interval, the error is at most a to the n, which is at most a to the N. So one cutoff works everywhere.

Narration: The cutoff may depend on our fixed endpoint a and on epsilon. It does not depend on x. Restricting the interval gives all points a shared distance from one, and therefore a shared error bound. That is the extra requirement hidden in uniform convergence.

plan.audience: Second-year mathematics students familiar with limits and epsilon notation.
prerequisites: Powers and roots of positive real numbers
plan.learningGoal: Distinguish the cutoff dependencies in pointwise and uniform convergence, construct a moving witness to nonuniform convergence of x^n on [0,1], and prove uniform convergence on [0,a] for fixed 0<a<1.
plan.centralQuestion: Why can a cutoff work for each fixed x without one cutoff working for every x, and how does restricting the interval change this?
plan.keyInsight: On [0,1], points depending on n retain error one half for arbitrarily large n, while on [0,a] every error is bounded by the single sequence a^n tending to zero.
plan.runningExample: f_n(x)=x^n for integers n≥1, first on [0,1] with limit f(x)=0 for x<1 and f(1)=1, then on [0,a], 0<a<1, with limit zero. Use ε=1/4, witnesses x_n=(1/2)^(1/n), and a=0.9 with N=14 as a numerical illustration only.
misconceptions: Pointwise cutoffs can always be replaced by one common cutoff.
The pointwise limit of x^n is zero at x=1.
The function value and convergence error coincide at the endpoint.
A changing x_n contradicts convergence at each fixed x.
Uniform convergence on each fixed [0,a] supplies one cutoff valid for every a<1.

entities.meaning: The two quantifier orders and common error inequality introduced in beat-1; retain their mathematical meaning when locally recalled in beat-4. The cutoff dependence changes, not the error test.

The horizontal x axis, domain, and shared unit scale introduced in beat-2, retained in beat-3 and restricted explicitly from [0,1] to [0,a] in beat-4. Vertical axis represents function values, with error segments measured in the same units.
The function x^n introduced in beat-2, retained through beat-4. Each curve and selected point must be calculated from the stated n, not geometrically morphed through unrelated curves.
The actual pointwise limit introduced in beat-2: zero below one and one at one. Preserve its open/filled endpoint distinction through beat-3; restrict it to zero on [0,a] in beat-4.

Distance between the power curve and actual pointwise limit, introduced in beat-2 and retained through beat-4. At x=1 on the original domain the distance is zero. Its supremum is one in beat-3 and a^n on the restricted domain in beat-4.

The selected point x_n=(1/2)^(1/n) introduced in beat-3, always below one with power value one half and limit value zero. As n changes, its horizontal position changes while its error remains one half; remove before the restricted-domain proof.
The fixed endpoint a<1 introduced in beat-4, default illustration a=0.9. It stays fixed while n increases; its function value a^n determines the shared error bound.

scenes.purpose: Make the quantifier order and permitted cutoff dependencies explicit.
scenes.whyNow: Opens with the definitions requested by the user and prepares the concrete power-sequence example.
keyPoints: State pointwise quantifiers with x before N.
State uniform quantifiers with N before x.
Identify the unchanged inequality and changed cutoff dependence.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because quantifier order and dependence are symbolic relations): On a black stage, introduce the pointwise definition, then the uniform definition, using short readable vector mathematics. Keep |f_n(x)-f(x)|<ε identical in the two statements. Locally emphasize x and N in order and annotate N(x,ε) versus N(ε). Do not suggest swapping quantifiers is an algebraic identity. These definitions are the opening content, not a title-card detour. Estimate roughly one minute of speech; measured audio determines actual duration.
scenes.endsWith: A settled comparison of the two definitions with the cutoff dependency legible; definition text then exits to prepare the concrete graph.

sourceRefs.supports: Requested opening definitions, audience, and quantifier comparison.

scenes.purpose: Derive the correct pointwise limit and distinguish value from error at the endpoint.
scenes.whyNow: Applies the definitions to x^n and supplies the exact limit needed for the subsequent uniform-error argument.
keyPoints: For each fixed x<1, x^n tends to zero.
At x=1 every value is one.
Error is x^n below one but zero at one.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because a scalar function and its domain are naturally planar): After the definitions exit, construct a shared coordinate scaffold with both axes spanning zero to one. Plot x^n for n=1,2,8,32 in sequence, calculating each curve from its exponent and retaining only enough previous curves to show the trend without clutter. Inspect x=1/2 with successive powers, then x=1 with constant value one. Derive and label the piecewise limit only after these two arguments. Show an open limit point at (1,0) and a filled point at (1,1); the blue curves all meet the filled endpoint. Introduce yellow vertical error segments joining corresponding graph and limit values below one. At one, explicitly show zero error without creating a spurious segment down to zero. Keep these same axes, functions, and units ready for beat-3. All graph annotations must fit the safe player area in 16:9 and 4:3.
scenes.endsWith: The n=32 power curve and actual piecewise limit share one scaffold, with the endpoint distinction clear and the error interpretation established. Earlier sample curves and inspection labels have exited.

sourceRefs.supports: Sequence x^n on [0,1], preservation of x=1, and distinction between pointwise limit and uniform error.

scenes.purpose: Disprove uniform convergence with a point chosen after the proposed exponent or cutoff.
scenes.whyNow: Uses the established limit and error rule to turn the quantifier comparison into a counterexample, preparing a search for a shared bound.
keyPoints: Construct x_n whose power value and error are one half.
Invite the one prediction and hold for five seconds.
For any N, n=N and x_N violate tolerance one quarter.
Explain the moving witness and supremum one without endpoint confusion.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because the counterexample is a relation between points, errors, and quantifiers on one graph): Continue the existing n=32 curve, limit, and scaffold. Introduce the point x_n=(1/2)^(1/n) and a yellow error segment of height one half, then show the same relation for a larger n using curves and witness coordinates computed from that n. Keep the limit endpoint at one intact. Place the ε=1/4 threshold so comparison with the half-height error is immediate. During the announced five-second pause, hold this evidence without displaying the words 'not uniform' or the quantified refutation. At Reveal, show an arbitrary proposed N paired with n=N and x_N, with the failing inequality. Then make clear that x_n moves while each fixed-point statement holds x constant. Show errors at points increasingly close to one approaching height one; their value at one itself remains zero. Label E_n=sup |x^n-f(x)|=1 and 'not attained' only after this reasoning. Remove the witness and temporary prediction annotations at the end; the error identity remains as the comparison state.
scenes.endsWith: The original graph, correct limit, and uniform-error value one remain. The moving witness has exited, leaving the near-one obstruction clear for domain restriction.

sourceRefs.supports: Explain why pointwise choices do not supply one cutoff; include one reachable prediction and brief pause. The root witness is an original derivation for the supplied sequence.

scenes.purpose: Prove uniform convergence on a fixed restricted interval using its maximal error.
scenes.whyNow: Resolves the near-one obstruction from beat-3 and concludes by identifying exactly which cutoff dependency changes.
keyPoints: Fix a<1 and visibly restrict the domain.
Choose N from a^N<ε and prove the bound for every n≥N and x≤a.
Conclude that N depends on a and ε but not x.
scenes.visualDescription: 2D (because the proof compares scalar errors on a restricted interval): Begin from the actual preceding graph and error annotation. Mark fixed a=0.9 on the existing axis, then remove the domain portion beyond a and its now-excluded endpoint while preserving the zero limit on the remaining domain. Exit the old supremum-one annotation before introducing the new bound. Show that the power curve is increasing in x for n≥1, with its largest vertical gap at a; label the same gap a^n and derive 0≤x^n≤a^n. Preserve the horizontal value a while increasing n and calculating both curve and bound together. For the continuing ε=1/4 example, indicate N=14 and 0.9^14≈0.229 only as a concrete illustration; the spoken general proof must remain primary. Reveal the inequality chain x^n≤a^n≤a^N<ε synchronized with the narration, then locally recall the uniform quantifiers and the permitted dependence N(a,ε). No interaction or extra prediction. Finish on the graph supporting the inequality rather than a detached recap card.
scenes.endsWith: The fixed restricted domain, its zero limit, a power curve below the tolerance, and the shared error bound form a stable final proof picture. The cutoff has no x dependence.

sourceRefs.supports: Requested proof on [0,a] for fixed 0<a<1 and explanation of why restriction fixes the failure.
